question.problem: What is the equation of the line that passes through the points $(1,-2)$ and $(3,6)$, expressed in standard form?
question.worked_solution:
First, we will construct the point-slope form of the line. Then, we will simplify it into standard form.

To construct the point-slope form of the line, we need a point and a slope. We already have two points, so we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\frac{6-(-2)}{3-1}=\frac{8}{2}=4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use this slope along with one of the points to write the point-slope form equation of the line. It doesn't matter which point we choose, but let's choose $(1,-2).$ The point-slope equation is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-2) & =4(x-1) \\ y+2 & =4(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we simplify the point-slope formula into standard form, moving the variables to the left side and the constant to the right side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2 & =4(x-1) \\ y+2 & =4x-4 \\ y & =4x-6 \\ -4x+y & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply by $-1$ to make the $x$-coefficient positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4x+y & =-6 \\ (-1)\cdot (-4x+y) & =(-1)\cdot (-6) \\ 4x-y & =6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the standard form of the equation is $4x-y=6.$
